query: For high-entropy nanoalloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve structural and chemical stability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a small amount of a refractory metal such as tungsten or molybdenum into the high-entropy nanoalloy composition can improve its structural and chemical stability at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy nanoalloy with a multi-principal element composition
generation.intervention: Addition of a refractory metal (e.g., tungsten or molybdenum) to the alloy composition
generation.conditions: High-temperature environment (above 800°C) for an extended period
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable, coherent nanoprecipitate or a solute-rich grain boundary phase
generation.mechanism: The refractory metal addition can slow down grain growth, reduce lattice distortion, and decrease the diffusion rates of other elements, thereby enhancing the alloy's resistance to oxidation, corrosion, and thermal degradation
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved structural stability (reduced grain growth, increased hardness) and chemical stability (reduced oxidation, improved corrosion resistance) relative to the baseline alloy without the refractory metal addition
generation.baseline: High-entropy nanoalloy without the refractory metal addition
generation.boundary: The refractory metal content should be below a certain threshold (e.g., 5 at.%) to avoid forming a separate, brittle intermetallic phase
generation.uncertainty: The optimal amount and type of refractory metal addition, as well as the potential interactions with other alloying elements, are uncertain and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy nanoalloy samples, one with and one without the refractory metal addition, and subject them to high-temperature annealing (e.g., 1000°C for 100 hours) in a controlled atmosphere
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with the refractory metal addition shows no significant improvement in structural and chemical stability compared to the baseline alloy, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization
